## 2. Exact statement that passes

Let `G=(V,E)` be any finite undirected loopless multigraph, with each parallel edge a distinct labelled coordinate, `|V|=2m>=2`, and at least one perfect matching. Let `P(G)` be the convex hull of its labelled perfect-matching incidence vectors. For **every** `x in P(G)` and **every** `v in V`, define, with natural logarithms and continuous endpoint products,

\[
H(x)=\max_{\mathbb E\mathbf1_M=x}\operatorname{Ent}(M),\qquad
F(x)=-\sum_e x_e\log x_e,\qquad
B(x)=-\sum_e(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e),
\]
\[
b_v(x)=-\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e),\qquad
W_v(x)=B(x)-b_v(x),\qquad D(x)=F(x)-H(x).
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{D_G(x)\le\tfrac32 W_{G,v}(x).}
\]

All boundary means, disconnected graphs, absent/unusable edges, forced edges, and finite labelled parallel multiplicities are included. A graph with no perfect matching has no feasible mean. The empty graph has `F=B=H=0`; it has no rooted assertion. No bound on degree or number of tight cuts is assumed. No finite-parameter exponential representation on **all** matchings is assumed at a boundary mean. No polynomial sampler or prescribed-mean optimizer is concluded.

## 3. Independent reconstruction of the full proof

### 3.1 The root reserve pays the separator exactly

Take an odd set `S` with both shores of size at least three and `x(delta(S))=1`. Complement it if needed so the designated root `v` lies in `S`; since the original order is even, its complement is also odd. Retain `S` in `G1`, contracting its complement; retain the complement in `G2`, contracting `S` to `z`. Discard edges wholly inside the contracted shore. Retain the original label on every surviving edge, including each crossing edge in **both** children. These operations create no loops; they may create parallel edges, which remain distinct. The child orders are even, at least four, and strictly smaller.

For every parent law with mean `x`, the crossing count is a positive odd integer with expectation one, hence equals one almost surely. Its two restrictions are child matchings with common crossing label `L`. Conversely, any two child matchings with the same crossing label glue uniquely to a parent matching crossing once. In particular the child means are feasible without any appeal to a relaxed polytope.

Write `q_e=x_e` on the cut, and let `h(q)` and `b(q)` be its categorical and complementary entropies. For every parent law, the chain rule and conditional subadditivity give

\[
\operatorname{Ent}(M)\le H_1(x_1)+H_2(x_2)-h(q).
\]

Choose maximizing laws at these **fixed** child means, whose crossing-label marginals both equal `q`. Draw `L~q` and, given `L`, draw the two child matchings independently from their respective conditional laws. This realizes the original mean and attains the displayed entropy. Terms with `q_e=0` require no conditional distribution. Thus

\[
H=H_1+H_2-h(q),\quad F=F_1+F_2-h(q),\quad
B=B_1+B_2-b(q),\quad D=D_1+D_2.
\]

The star at the retained root in `G1` has the same labelled coordinates as the parent root star. The star at `z` in `G2` is exactly the cut. Therefore

\[
W_v=B_1+B_2-b(q)-b_v
=(B_1-b_v)+(B_2-b_z)=W_{1,v}+W_{2,z}.
\]

It follows for every real `c` that

\[
(D-cW)_{G,v}=(D-cW)_{G_1,v}+(D-cW)_{G_2,z}. \tag{R2-A}
\]

This is an exact identity, not an inequality with an omitted separator. Edge by edge: a crossing edge incident to the root is uncharged in both children, while any other crossing edge is charged once in `G1` and uncharged in `G2`. An internal edge is charged in its one retained child exactly when it was charged in the parent.

An inherited root may itself have been created by an earlier contraction. Nothing above requires it to be an original vertex: it is an ordinary vertex of the current loopless labelled graph, with its actual star. Inductively, arbitrary further valid splits telescope (R2-A). No laminar ordering of all original tight cuts is necessary. Strictly decreasing child orders make the recursion finite. In particular, the sum of leaf root-star reserves equals the original reserve plus the sum of all split complementary entropies. This resolves the precise positive-separator objection in I22.

### 3.2 Parallel labels and the small-order base

For each parallel class `C_a`, put `y_a=sum_{e in C_a}x_e<=1` and, when `y_a>0`, `r^a_e=x_e/y_a`. A labelled matching specifies a collapsed matching `Y` and a chosen label in each selected class. Conditional entropy is at most the sum of the label entropies. Averaging over `Y` and using concavity gives an upper bound `sum_a y_a h(r^a)` for the extra entropy: the aggregate conditional label distribution, given that a class is selected, is precisely `r^a`. A maximizing collapsed law with independent label choices of these distributions attains the upper bound. Consequently

\[
H_G(x)=H_{\rm simple}(y)+\sum_a y_a h(r^a),\qquad
F_G(x)=F_{\rm simple}(y)+\sum_a y_a h(r^a).
\]

Thus `D` is invariant. A zero class contributes zero and is simply ignored. For `beta(u)=-(1-u)log(1-u)`, concavity and `beta(0)=0` imply `beta(x_e)>=x_e beta(y_a)/y_a` within a positive class. Summing proves `sum beta(x_e)>=beta(y_a)`. Each class is wholly incident or wholly nonincident to a given root, so `W_G,v>=W_simple,v`. The inequality transfers from collapsed to labelled graphs in the required direction for nonnegative `c`; there is no illicit cancellation of label entropy in `B`.

On two vertices, `F=H` and `W_v=0`, however many parallel labels exist. On four vertices, after collapse and padding missing edges by zero, the three possible perfect-matching types are disjoint pairs of edges. A feasible mean determines their probabilities `p=(p1,p2,p3)`. For each root one of each type's two edges is incident to it. Hence `H=h(p)`, `F=2h(p)`, `D=h(p)`, and `W_v=b(p)`.

For completeness, the scalar inequality `h(p)<=3b(p)/2` really does hold on the entire closed ternary simplex. Set

\[
f(u)=-u\log u+\tfrac32(1-u)\log(1-u),\qquad
f''(u)=-1/u+\tfrac{3/2}{1-u}.
\]

The second derivative changes sign at `a=2/5`. On the simplex boundary, `sum f=(1-3/2)h(p,1-p)<=0`. At an interior maximum all first derivatives agree. Two coordinates at least `a`, one strictly above, violate the second derivative test along their difference; two equal to `a` violate stationarity with the smaller third coordinate. If all coordinates are at most `a`, strict decrease of `f'` forces equality, giving `sum f=log(8/9)<0`. Otherwise exactly one is above `a`, and the other two are equal below `a`; write the vector as `(t,t,1-2t)`, where `0<t<1/3`.

For `g(t)=2f(t)+f(1-2t)` and `u=(1-2t)/t>=1`,

\[
g'(t)/2=\log u-\tfrac32\log((u+1)/2)=k(u),\qquad
k'(u)=\frac{1-u/2}{u(u+1)}.
\]

The function `k` rises from zero, then falls to minus infinity, with exactly one further zero. Because `u` decreases with `t`, `g` first decreases and then increases. Its maximum on `[0,1/3]` is at an endpoint, whose values are `0` and `log(8/9)`. This covers every remaining possibility for a positive maximum and proves the scalar inequality. Therefore the two- and four-vertex rooted bases pass for all means and labelled multiplicities. They also hold for every `c>3/2`, since `W>=0`.

### 3.3 Boundary reductions, including loss of the root

Delete every zero-mean edge. Every law at that mean omits it, and its contributions to `F`, `B`, and each root star vanish. More strongly, every feasible mean of the resulting graph zero-extends to a mean of the original graph with the same objective. Thus a global maximizer remains a global maximizer after this operation, even though order has not decreased.

If an edge has mean one, every realizing law contains it. All other edges at its two endpoints have mean zero. Delete those endpoints and the forced edge. The source's bijection of laws preserves `F,H,B`, and the remaining order strictly decreases. If the root survives, its nonzero star coordinates survive and `W` is unchanged. If the root is deleted, its entire complementary star entropy was zero, so the original `W_v=B`. For any residual root `w`, the smaller rooted assertion yields

\[
D=D_{\rm residual}\le c(B-b_w)\le cB=cW_v.
\]

If no vertices remain, all these quantities are zero. This argument needs only a smaller-order inequality at the residual mean; it does **not** need to transfer global maximality to a different residual-root objective. That distinction prevents a possible deleted-root circularity.

### 3.4 Attainment, face laws, and the modified trace

For a fixed finite graph and root, `E_c=F-cW_v-H` is continuous on compact `P(G)`, so it attains a maximum. The source's continuity statement is global, not just relative-interior continuity: compactness of the law simplex gives upper semicontinuity; the finite inequality description and mixing along an extendible segment give lower semicontinuity. Thus a boundary maximizing sequence cannot evade attainment.

At a point with all retained coordinates in `(0,1)`, let `T` be its minimal-face tangent space and `d=dim T`. The maximizing law is positive on **all face atoms** and has a finite exponential parameter `theta` on those atoms. One can see positivity by mixing with a full-support law of the same mean; a previously zero probability increases entropy by a positive `t log(1/t)` term. Stationarity of entropy in the law fiber gives the exponential representation even with redundant constraints. Its covariance `K` has kernel `T^perp`, since zero variance means a linear functional is constant on the affinely spanning face atoms. Therefore `im K=T` and `rank K=d`.

Tilt the face law by `theta+ta` and denote its mean by `y(t)`. The same finite Gibbs variational comparison makes it entropy maximizing at its own mean; it remains in the same minimal face. Hence

\[
y'(0)=Ka,\quad y''(0)\in T,\qquad
H(y(t))=\log Z(\theta+ta)-(\theta+ta)\cdot y(t).
\]

For `J=F-cW_v`, its diagonal Hessian is

\[
A_{ee}=-1/x_e+\frac{c\,\mathbf1_{e\notin\delta(v)}}{1-x_e}.
\]

At a local maximum of `E_c`, both signs of every tilt are feasible and

\[
0=E_c'(0)=(\nabla J+\theta)\cdot Ka\qquad\text{for all }a.
\]

The vector `grad J+theta` is thus orthogonal to `T`, so the acceleration term vanishes in the second derivative:

\[
0\ge E_c''(0)=(Ka)^TA(Ka)+a^TKa.
\]

For positive covariance eigenvalues `lambda_i` and orthonormal eigenvectors `u_i`, substitute `a=u_i`, divide by `lambda_i`, and sum. This gives

\[
0\ge d+\operatorname{tr}(KA).
\]

It neither inverts an ambient covariance kernel nor assumes that `A` and `K` commute. Since each coordinate is Boolean, `K_ee=x_e(1-x_e)`. The degree equations give `sum_e x_e=m` and, critically, `sum_{e not incident to v}x_e=m-1`. With `s=|E|`,

\[
\boxed{0\ge d-s+m+c(m-1).} \tag{R2-T}
\]

The root term costs exactly `c` relative to the source's unrooted trace. Its coefficient is not guessed by substituting a new objective into an old theorem. The calculation uses smooth finite tilts only, so it does not demand smoothness of `H` across different faces.

### 3.5 The induction is global and closes for every graph

Fix any `epsilon>0` and put `c=3/2+epsilon`. Induct on `m` with the simultaneous assertion for **every graph of order `2m`, every mean, every root**, using the same constant `c` at all smaller orders. Sections 3.2–3.3 establish the small-order and fixed-coordinate steps.

Suppose there is a counterexample at order `2m`, `m>=3`. For that particular finite graph and that particular root, maximize `E_c` on its polytope; the maximum is positive. No maximization over the class of all graphs or edge multiplicities is required. Delete zero edges, preserving the positive global maximum. A value-one edge would reduce to a smaller-order instance and contradict positivity, so all retained coordinates lie strictly between zero and one.

If a nontrivial odd cut is tight at this maximum, its two child orders are smaller. Both rooted inequalities are available at the restricted means by induction, irrespective of whether those means optimize any child objective. Identity (R2-A) then says the parent defect is nonpositive. Thus **there is no nontrivial tight odd cut at the positive global maximum**. This is the justified point where the stronger dimension estimate becomes available.

Positivity leaves no active nonnegativity rows. Singleton odd cuts and their complements are the degree rows. All other odd-cut inequalities have strict slack. Because the graph is finite, there are finitely many such inequalities, and sufficiently small two-sided perturbations preserving degrees remain feasible. Therefore `T` is the kernel of the `2m` degree rows, and `d>=s-2m`. Redundancy, bipartite components, and disconnectedness can only increase this lower bound; row independence is unnecessary.

Combining with (R2-T),

\[
0\ge d-s+m+c(m-1)
\ge(c-1)m-c
=\frac{m-3}{2}+\epsilon(m-1)>0,
\]

a contradiction for every `m>=3`. This proves the assertion at coefficient `3/2+epsilon` for every order and root. For any fixed `G,x,v`, the finite sum `W_v` is nonnegative and finite. Taking `epsilon` down to zero gives `D<=3W_v/2`, including `W_v=0`. No uniform bound across all graphs or convergence of maximizing points is required. The epsilon step is essential to this particular proof at `m=3`: the endpoint trace lower bound alone is zero, not contradictory.

This completes a universal proof. It is not an inference from the finite numerical audit.

## 4. Ancillary Section 6: Klee local maxima

The source gives a minimal face with three disjoint matching types of size `m`, partitioning all `3m` edges. On its relative interior, a mean specifies a unique type law `p`. Hence

\[
H=h(p),\quad F=mh(p),\quad B=mb(p),\qquad
E_{3/2}=(m-1)h(p)-\tfrac32m b(p).
\]

At the uniform type law,

\[
E_{3/2}=m\log(8/9)-\log3<0.
\]

For a tangent probability perturbation `sum a_i=0`, the second derivative is `(3-3m/4)sum a_i^2`. Thus for every integer `m>4` the point is a strict face-local maximum. The edge covariance has entries `2/9` within one type and `-1/9` between types, rank two, and positive eigenvalues `m/3`. The separable Hessian is `-3I/4`; on positive covariance eigenvectors the normalized second variation is `1-m/4<0`. These calculations check the full tangent matrix inequality, not just its trace. Every star and every tight-cut sum is constant on the three atoms, so the global matching constraints are respected.

The candidate's extension to a strict local maximum in the **whole polytope** is also correct. To make its uniform estimates explicit, let `ell` be the sum of finitely many active nonnegative slacks exposing this face. If there are outside atoms, let `delta>0` be the minimum of `ell` over them. For any nearby mean `x'` and any realizing law, its outside mass `r` satisfies `r<=ell(x')/delta`, hence tends to zero uniformly as `x'` approaches the uniform face mean `x`. For `r<1`, condition on the face and call the conditional mean `y`. Then `y` tends to `x` uniformly, and `||x'-y||<=C0 r` because the polytope is bounded.

The face law at `y` is unique, so that conditional law has entropy `H(y)` even if the original realizing law was not maximizing. Consequently

\[
H(x')\ge h_2(r)+(1-r)H(y).
\]

The function `J=F-3B/2` is Lipschitz near `x`, since every coordinate of `x` equals `1/3`. Also `H(y)<=log3`. It follows that

\[
E(x')\le E(y)+Cr-h_2(r).
\]

For all sufficiently small positive `r`, `h_2(r)>Cr`. Choose the neighborhood small enough that `y` lies in the strict face-maximum neighborhood. If `r>0`, the last display is strictly below `E(x)`; if `r=0` and `x'!=x`, strict face maximality applies. If there are no outside atoms, the face proof alone suffices. Thus the claimed full local assertion passes with uniform constants, not just along individual transverse curves.

This is ancillary and not used to prove the theorem. It explains why attempting to exclude **all** fractional local maxima would fail: these maxima have negative defect, while matching vertices have defect zero. On these same faces `D=(m-1)h(p)` and `W_v=(m-1)b(p)`. The uniform rooted ratio is the old `c3=log3/[2log(3/2)]` for `m>1`, not a new numerical obstruction.

## 5. Section 9 and other consequences

All stated implications pass with their indicated scope.

First, `sum_v b_v=2B`, since an edge has two distinct endpoints. With `2m` vertices, `max_v b_v>=B/m`. The assertion for **every** root allows selection of a maximizing root at each mean, yielding

\[
H\ge F-\tfrac32(B-\max_v b_v)
\ge F-\tfrac32(1-1/m)B
\ge F-\tfrac32 B.
\]

The inequalities have the right direction, including `m=1` and `B=0`. Next `beta(u)<=u` on `[0,1]`, so `W_v<=sum_{e not incident to v}x_e=m-1`. Thus `0<=D<=3(m-1)/2`; the lower inequality is the source's star-chain-rule upper bound `H<=F`.

For every finite real edge parameter `theta`, the finite Gibbs variational identity gives

\[
\log Z_\theta=\max_{x\in P(G)}[H(x)+\theta\cdot x].
\]

Let `Q_theta=max[F+theta dot x]`. The pointwise two-sided bound just proved gives

\[
Q_\theta-\tfrac32(m-1)\le\log Z_\theta\le Q_\theta.
\]

The extrema are attained by compactness. The bracket is analytic and uses natural logarithms; converting the source's binary-log version introduces no extra coefficient here. It does not assert computational access to either maximizing mean or exponential law.

For `k>=2` edge-disjoint labelled perfect matchings, their uniform mixture has `km` nonzero edge coordinates equal to `1/k`. Each root sees exactly `k` of them. Thus `F=m log k` and

\[
W_v=(m-1)(k-1)\log\frac{k}{k-1}.
\]

Using `log N>=H` and exponentiating gives exactly

\[
N(G)\ge k^m(1-1/k)^{(3/2)(m-1)(k-1)}
\ge k^m e^{-(3/2)(m-1)}.
\]

The coarse inequality follows from `(k-1)log(1-1/k)>=-1`. Extra ambient edges have zero coordinates in the selected mixture and cause no problem. For a `k`-regular graph with all odd cuts of size at least `k`, the uniform vector satisfies the full matching-polytope constraints, so exactly the same substitution applies without an edge partition. The formula involving `1/k` is asserted for `k>=2`; at `k=1` the graph itself is a matching. Empty graphs are handled separately.

After zero/fixed-coordinate deletion, residual components have even order and their matching laws form a Cartesian product. Conditional subadditivity gives the entropy upper bound by the sum of component maxima; independent maximizing component laws attain it. Hence `D` is additive across components and the componentwise rooted consequence is valid.

Finally, the six-vertex suggestion is correctly conditional. If a rooted `c3` theorem were established there, the two-/four-vertex `c3` bases plus the same induction would handle all larger orders, since for `m>=4`, `(c3-1)m-c3>=3c3-4>0`; indeed `3c3-4=log(256/243)/(2log(3/2))`. No six-vertex `c3` proof or optimality claim follows from the present argument. The old source examples give the unrooted universal lower limit `c3`; the rooted lower bound already occurs at `K4`.

## 6. Adversarial challenges: disposition

- **Unpaid positive separator:** resolved by exact identity (R2-A), for labelled crossing edges and arbitrary compatible maximizing child laws. The unrooted separator term in I22 remains positive; it is paid, not discarded.
- **Root reserve exhausted after several splits:** resolved by propagation of the actual retained root and rooting the other child at its contraction vertex. The edgewise identity holds again when a root was itself contracted earlier.
- **Circular leaf theorem or unjustified choice of a favorable leaf maximum:** resolved by strong induction on vertex count, uniform over all smaller graphs/means/roots. Child maxima are never assumed. A single positive parent global maximum is used.
- **General face rank still only proves coefficient two:** resolved only after positivity and induction exclude every nontrivial tight cut. Applying `d>=s-2m` before that point would be invalid; the candidate applies it afterward.
- **Boundary maximum or unbounded exponential parameters:** resolved by attained continuous `H`, zero/one reductions, and the finite exponential representation on the minimal face, not on the ambient matching set.
- **Deleted root, disconnected graph, or two-vertex parallel component:** resolved by Section 3.3 and the two-vertex base. No connectedness hypothesis is introduced.
- **Parallel collapse loses label entropy or root identity:** resolved by exact equal increments in `F,H`, complementary-entropy monotonicity, and classwise root incidence.
- **Stationarity fails in constrained directions; acceleration was silently ignored:** resolved by `im K=T`, stationarity for all exponential tilts, and `y'' in T`. No simultaneous diagonalization is used.
- **Six vertices at exactly `c=3/2`:** resolved by proving every strict coefficient first, then taking the pointwise endpoint limit. The endpoint trace alone does not suffice.
- **Klee transverse directions invalidate a face-local statement:** resolved by the exposing-slack mass bound and the `h_2(r)` entropy gain. This ancillary assertion is stronger than the tangent calculation and has been checked separately.
- **Finite Gibbs tests are mistaken for universal proof:** resolved by the all-order proof above. Numerical records support only their finite, explicitly specified instances.

**Unresolved mathematical objections to the stated rooted theorem: none found. Required repairs: none.** Open issues outside this verdict remain optimality of `3/2`, the conditional six-vertex `c3` improvement, computational prescribed-mean access, and independent significance/prior-art assessment.

Their [permanent approximation theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11049v1) concerns weighted bipartite counts. Neither inspected interface substitutes for the rooted lower-bound proof.

 6.3   Perfect matchings in r-graphs and the Lovász–Plummer conjecture
Theorem 5.4 has a consequence for the number of perfect matchings in certain graphs. To elaborate, let r ≥ 3 be
an integer. An r-graph is an r-regular graph G = (V, E) where |V | is even, and every odd cut has size at least r,
that is, |δ(U )| ≥ r for all U ⊂ V where |U | is odd. It is known that every r-graph is matching-covered, that is,
every edge belongs to a perfect matching [Sey79]. A well-known conjecture by Lovász and Plummer states that
for every r ≥ 3, there exist constants c1 (r) > 1, c2 (r) > 0 such that every r-regular matching-covered graph
G = (V, E) contains at least c2 (r) · c1 (r)|V | perfect matchings; furthermore, c1 (r) → ∞ as r → ∞ [[LP86],
Conjecture 8.1.8]. The first part of this conjecture was proved for 3-graphs [EKK+ 11]. In this subsection, we
prove (a refinement of) this part for all r-graphs for r ≥ 4.
    Perfect matchings intersecting every minimum odd cut exactly once correspond to the core of a certain ideal
r-cover-minimal clutter. Through this connection, we shall prove the following as a consequence of Theorem 5.4.
Theorem 6.3. For every integer r ≥ 3 and β ∈ (0, 1), there is a constant θ := θ1.2 (r, β) > 0 such that the
following statement holds:
    Let G = (V, E) be an r-graph where the rank of {1δ(U ) : |δ(U )| = r, |U | is odd} is at most (1 − β)|E|.
Then the number of perfect matchings of G that intersect every minimum odd cut exactly once is at least eθ|E| .
Proof. A postman set is a subset J ⊆ E where every vertex of G is incident to an odd number of edges from J.
Let C be the clutter over ground set E of the minimal postman sets of G. It is known that C is an ideal clutter,
and that b(C) consists of the minimal odd cuts of G [EJ73]. In particular, as G is an r-graph, C is an r-cover-
minimal clutter, and core(C) is precisely the clutter of perfect matchings of G that intersect every minimum odd
cut exactly once. The claim now follows from Theorem 5.4 for θ := θ1.2 (r, β).
    By applying Theorem 3.2 to a different polytope, Barvinok showed that every 3-graph G = (V, E) that is
essentially 4-edge-connected, i.e., |δ(U )| ≥ 4 for all U ⊂ V such that 1 < |U | < |V | − 1, has exponentially
many perfect matchings [Bar13]. Observe that in this case, the rank of {1δ(U ) : |δ(U )| = 3, |U | is odd} is at
most |V | = 32 |E|, so we can also apply Theorem 6.3 for r = 3, β = 13 to obtain this result.
    Using graph theoretic techniques, Esperet et al. showed that the number of perfect matchings in any 3-graph
G = (V, E) is at least 2|V |/3656 . The authors then used this result to show that every   (r − 1)-edge-connected
r-graph for r ≥ 4, has at least 2f (r)·|V | perfect matchings for f (r) = 3656
                                                                            1
                                                                               1 − 1r 1 − 2r [EKK+ 11].
                                                                                     

    It turns out that for r ≥ 4, all r-graphs satisfy the rank condition in Theorem 6.3. To see this, we need a few
notions and lemmas. A family L over ground set V is laminar if for all U, W ∈ L such that U ∩ W ̸= ∅, we
have U ⊆ W or W ⊆ U . A simple inductive argument implies that a laminar family L has size at most 2|V | − 1.
However, this upper bound can be improved in the following relevant case.
Lemma 6.4. Let L be a laminar family of odd subsets of {1, . . . , 2n}. Then |L| ≤ 3n − 1.
Proof. We prove this by induction on n. The base case n = 1 is clear. For the induction step, assume that n ≥ 2.
    Suppose in the first case that some maximal set A in L has size ≤ 2n − 3. We may clearly assume that
|A| ≥ 3. Let B := A. Then |B| is odd, and L ∪ {B} is also laminar, so we may assume that B ∈ L. Let L1 , L2
be obtained from L after shrinking B, A to a single element b, a, respectively. Observe that L1 contains both A
and {b}, and L2 contains both B and {a}. Given that the ground set of each Li has 2ni < 2n elements, we can
apply the induction hypothesis to conclude that

      |L| = |L1 | + |L2 | − 2 ≤ (3n1 − 1) + (3n2 − 1) − 2 = 3(n1 + n2 ) − 4 = 3(n + 1) − 4 = 3n − 1,

thus completing the induction step in this case.
    Suppose in the remaining case that every maximal set in L has size 2n − 1. Thus, there is a unique maximal
set A in L. Now, let B be a proper maximal subset of A in L, which we may assume exists and satisfies |B| ≥ 3.
By definition, |B| ≤ |A| − 2. Then L′ := (L \ {A}) ∪ {B} is also laminar family of odd subsets of {1, . . . , 2n}.
Furthermore, B is a maximal set in L′ of size ≤ 2n − 3. Therefore, by falling back to the previous case, we
obtain that |L| = |L′ | ≤ 3n − 1, thus completing the induction step.

                                                           APPROXIMATION OF THE PERMANENT

                                                                            DINGDING DONG AND VISHESH JAIN


                                                 Abstract. For an n × n nonnegative matrix A, the Bethe permanent, which is computable in
                                                 deterministic polynomial time, satisfies the tight universal comparison
                                                                                Bethe(A) ≤ per(A) ≤ 2n/2 Bethe(A).

    The lower and upper bounds are attained at opposite extremes. On tree-structured graphical
models, the Bethe approximation is exact [23]. For perfect matchings, this follows directly. A forest
has at most one perfect matching, since the symmetric difference of two perfect matchings would
contain a cycle. Moreover, if a perfect matching exists, repeated deletion of leaves shows that its
indicator vector is the unique point of PM(GA ). Hence Bethe(A) = per(A) whenever GA is a forest.
By contrast, equality in (1.5) is obtained by the bipartite adjacency matrix of a disjoint union of
4-cycles, the shortest possible cycles in a bipartite graph.
1.3. Our contribution. The contrast between forests and 4-cycles suggests that the error of the
Bethe approximation should be controlled by the girth of the support graph. Recall that the girth
of a graph is the length of its shortest cycle (which is necessarily even for a bipartite graph), with
forests regarded as having infinite girth. Motivated by this, Nima Anari proposed the following

Theorem 1.3. Let g ≥ 4 be even, and let A ∈ Rn×n ≥0 be a nonnegative matrix whose support graph
has girth at least g. Then

are disjoint unions of cycles of length g.

extreme, the Bethe approximation is exact on forests, as discussed above. More generally, along
any sequence of matrices whose support graphs have girth tending to infinity, the Bethe permanent
approximates the permanent within a subexponential factor.
1.4. Relation to previous work. As discussed above, the Bethe permanent is exact when the
support graph is a forest. This is consistent with the more general exactness of the Bethe ap-
proximation on tree-structured graphical models [23]. On graphs with cycles, loop calculus gives
exact formulas for the discrepancy between the true partition function and its Bethe approxima-
tion. Chertkov and Chernyak [7] expressed the partition function as the Bethe contribution plus
correction terms indexed by generalized loops, and Watanabe and Chertkov [22] derived a version of
                                                  3

loops and their weights. By contrast, Theorem 1.3 gives a sharp worst-case bound depending only
on the girth of the support graph.

related models on graph sequences that become locally tree-like; see, for example, [5, 10, 17, 24]. In
the setting of perfect matchings, Abért, Csikvári, Frenkel, and Kun [1] showed that for d-regular
bipartite graphs converging locally to the d-regular tree, the normalized logarithm of the number
of perfect matchings converges to the Bethe prediction; see also Lelarge [15] for related results. In
the other direction, Csikvári [9] showed that for d-regular vertex-transitive bipartite graphs, the
presence of a cycle of bounded length gives a strict exponential improvement over this tree rate.
The former results concern locally tree-like limits or finite-activity models, while Csikvári’s result
requires regularity and vertex transitivity. By contrast, Theorem 1.3 gives a sharp non-asymptotic
bound for weighted perfect matchings without any additional assumptions.

                                                                NONNEGATIVE MATRIX

                                                                           DINGDING DONG AND VISHESH JAIN


                                                 Abstract. For every fixed 0 < ε ≤ 1, we give a deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm that,
                                                 given a nonnegative matrix A ∈ Rn×n                                          n
                                                                                 ≥0 , returns Q satisfying per A ≤ Q ≤ (1 + ε) per A.

                                         the bipartite support graph of A when A is a 0–1 matrix. For Q    general nonnegative A, it is the total
                                         weight of perfect matchings, where a matching M has weight ij∈M Aij .
                                            Valiant [27] proved that computing the permanent is #P-complete even for 0–1 matrices. On the
                                         algorithmic side, Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda [18] gave a fully polynomial randomized approximation
                                         scheme for nonnegative matrices. The existence of a deterministic (fully) polynomial approximation
                                         scheme remains a major open problem.
                                            The known deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for general nonnegative matrices have
                                         approximation factors exponential in n. Throughout, we measure multiplicative guarantees by
                                         the width of a certified interval, i.e., a factor C ≥ 1 approximation consists of polynomial-time
                                         computable quantities L(A) and U (A) satisfying
                                                                   L(A) ≤ per(A) ≤ U (A)            and       U (A) ≤ CL(A).
                                         Linial, Samorodnitsky, and Wigderson [21] obtained a factor en by combining matrix scaling with
                                         the van der Waerden inequality. Subsequent improvements used the Bethe permanent, which can be
                                         computed by convex optimization [28]. Gurvits [15] proved that the Bethe permanent is a lower

in Section 1.1. The running time can be improved to nO(ε log (2/ε)) by replacing the map used in
Section 3 with the rational map in [4, Lemma 2.3]. We do not pursue this refinement here.

1.1. Computational model. We use the arithmetic model of [21], in which additions, subtractions,
multiplications, divisions, and exact comparisons of real numbers have unit cost. An algorithm is
strongly polynomial if its operation count is polynomial in the number of input entries, independently
of their magnitudes and encoding lengths, and if, on rational inputs, all numbers computed have bit
lengths polynomial in the total input length. We apply this definition with ε fixed.
   The bit length of a rational number r, denoted as ℓ(r), is the sum of the binary lengths of
its numerator and denominator in lowest terms. Elementary functions are evaluated by rational
approximation, with the cost included in the operation count.

1.2. Related work. Gamarnik and Katz [13] obtained a (1 + ε)n approximation for 0–1 matrices in
polynomial time under the assumption that the support graph has bounded maximum degree and
vertex expansion bounded away from zero. For arbitrary 0–1 matrices, their algorithm achieves the
same approximation factor in time exp(O(ε−1/2 n2/3 log3 n)). Their algorithm uses the approximation
scheme of Bayati, Gamarnik, Katz, Nair, and Tetali [8] for the matching partition function M λ|M | ,
                                                                                                P
where the sum is over all matchings. For fixed activity λ and bounded maximum degree, these
authors gave a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme based on correlation decay.
Gamarnik and Katz use vertex expansion to bound the contribution of nonperfect matchings when
λ is sufficiently large.
   For matrices satisfying a ≤ Aij ≤ 1 for all i, j, where a > 0 is fixed, matrix scaling gives
a polynomial-factor approximation in polynomial time [21, 7]. Barvinok obtained more accurate
approximations in quasipolynomial time, first for real or complex matrices whose entries are sufficiently
close to 1 [5], and subsequently for all real matrices satisfying a ≤ Aij ≤ 1 [6]. In the latter setting,
his algorithm approximates log per A to additive error ζ ∈ (0, 1) in time nOa (log n+log(1/ζ)) . Recently,
Yi [30] gave an FPTAS for matrices with entries in {0} ∪ [a, 1], where a > 0 is fixed, provided every
row and column has at least (1/2 + γ)n nonzero entries for a fixed γ > 0.
   Barvinok’s algorithms use his interpolation method, which approximates the logarithm of a
polynomial from its firstP few    coefficients, using bounds on the locations of its zeros. For the
polynomial ZG (z) =         z |M | , where the sum is over all matchings of G, the Heilmann–Lieb
                          M
theorem [17] places all zeros on the negative real axis. Barvinok [4] used this to approximate the
total number of matchings from the first few coefficients of ZG . Patel and Regts [25] showed how to
compute the required coefficients efficiently on bounded-degree graphs, obtaining polynomial-time
approximation algorithms from suitable bounds on the zeros. We refer to [3] for a general account of
this method.
   The Bethe permanent is computable by convex optimization [28] and is a lower bound for the
permanent [15]. The authors [12] proved that its approximation factor improves from 2n/2 to 22n/g
if the support graph has girth at least g, for even g ≥ 4. This comparison is sharp and holds for
arbitrary nonnegative edge weights.

Independent work. After finishing this paper and right before submitting it, we learned of
independent work of Kudria, Luo, and Majid [20] which provides an exp(o(n))-factor approximation
of the permanent in deterministic polynomial time. We believe that by replacing the exact Taylor
polynomial in Section 3 by a suitable approximation, our algorithm can also be modified to achieve
this guarantee.

The results from running BP-Bootstrap on sparse complete graph instances are shown in Table 1.
For each number of nodes N ∈ {100, 250, 500, 1000}, we generated 100 random instances. We report
the average number of edges, M , for each setting of N and # Cor., the number of instances (out of
100) for which BP-Bootstrap found the optimal weight matching. In addition, we report the average
and [minimum, maximum] number of LP s solved by BP-Bootstrap as well as the number of blossoms
contracted by the BP-Bootstrap procedure. From this table it seems clear that BP-Bootstrap procedure is
accurate on dense complete graphs. A reason for the success of the method on this class of graphs is that
LP (0) , the initial LP relaxation, is tight a large percentage of the time. This is indicated by the fact that
on average less than two LP s need to be solved by BP-Bootstrap.
    In contrast, the Bootstrap method performs rather poorly on the random Triangulation instances
shown in Table 2. The greedy blossom contracting approach does not appear to be successful on this
class of problems. In fact, when we examined the operation of Kolmogorov’s BlossomV algorithm on
these instances we found that BlossomV frequently needed to backtrack and expand blossoms that had
been collapsed - an operation not supported by our greedy heuristic.
    Finally, the results from running BP-Bootstrap on the chained triangle instances are shown in Table
3. The BP-Bootstrap method performs well on these problems. Interestingly, we see that the greedy
heuristic is effective even though these instances require solving many LP s and collapsing many
blossoms.

                                                                                       Abstract
                                                 We give a deterministic polynomial time 2O(r )-approximation algorithm for the number of
                                             bases of a given matroid of rank r and the number of common bases of any two matroids of
                                             rank r. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first nontrivial deterministic approximation
                                             algorithm that works for arbitrary matroids. Based on a lower bound of Azar, Broder, and
                                             Frieze [ABF94] this is almost the best possible result assuming oracle access to independent
                                             sets of the matroid.
                                                 There are two main ingredients in our result: For the first, we build upon recent results
                                             of Adiprasito, Huh, and Katz [AHK15] and Huh and Wang [HW17] on combinatorial hodge
                                             theory to derive a connection between matroids and log-concave polynomials. We expect that
                                             several new applications in approximation algorithms will be derived from this connection
                                             in future. Formally, we prove that the multivariate generating polynomial of the bases of
                                             any matroid is log-concave as a function over the positive orthant. For the second ingredient,
                                             we develop a general framework for approximate counting in discrete problems, based on
                                             convex optimization. The connection goes through subadditivity of the entropy. For matroids,
                                             we prove that an approximate superadditivity of the entropy holds by relying on the log-
                                             concavity of the corresponding polynomials.

Counting and Sampling Perfect Matchings
                                                        in Regular Expanding Non-Bipartite Graphs

                                                         Farzam Ebrahimnejad∗, Ansh Nagda†, and Shayan Oveis Gharan‡




arXiv:2103.08683v1 [cs.DS] 15 Mar 2021
                                                                                University of Washington


                                                                                       March 17, 2021



                                                                                            Abstract
                                                   We show that the ratio of the number of near perfect matchings to the number of perfect
                                               matchings in 𝑑-regular strong expander (non-bipartite) graphs, with 2𝑛 vertices, is a polynomial
                                               in 𝑛, thus the Jerrum and Sinclair Markov chain [JS89] mixes in polynomial time and generates
                                               an (almost) uniformly random perfect matching. Furthermore, we prove that such graphs have
                                               at least Ω(𝑑)𝑛 many perfect matchings, thus proving the Lovasz-Plummer conjecture [LP86] for
                                               this family of graphs.




                                           ∗ febrahim@cs.washington.edu Research supported in part by NFS grant CCF-1552097.
                                           † ansh@cs.washington.edu
                                           ‡ shayan@cs.washington.edu. Research supported by Air Force Oﬃce of Scientiﬁc Research grant FA9550-20-1-0212,
                                         NSF grants CCF-1552097, CCF-1907845, and a Sloan fellowship.
 1 Introduction
Given a (general) graph 𝐺 = (𝑉 , 𝐸) with 2𝑛 = |𝑉 | vertices, the problem of counting the number
of perfect matchings in 𝐺 is one of the most fundamental open problems in the ﬁeld of counting.
Jerrum and Sinclair in their landmark result [JS89] designed a Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC)
algorithm for this task and proved that such an algorithm runs in polynomial time if the ratio of the
number of near perfect matchings to the number of perfect matchings is bound by a polynomial
(in 𝑛). As a consequence one would be able to count perfect matchings if 𝐺 is very dense, i.e., it has
min-degree at least 𝑛. Not much is known beyond this case, despite several exciting results when
the given graph 𝐺 is bipartite [JV96; LSW00; Bar99; JSV04; Bez+06].
    This problem is also extensively studied in combinatorics. Around 40 years ago, Falikman
and Egorychev [Ego81; Fal81] proved the van-der-Waerden conjecture, thus showing that if 𝐺 is
a 𝑑-regular bipartite graph, then it has at least (𝑑/𝑒)𝑛 perfect matchings. This bound was further
improved by Schrĳver [Sch98] and simpler and more general proofs were found [Gur06; AOV21].
But it remains a mystery whether van-der-Waerden conjecture extends to non-bipartite graphs.
Lovasz, Plummer most famously made the following conjecture:
Conjecture 1.1 ([LP86, Conjecture 8.1.8]). For 𝑑 ≥ 3, there exist constants 𝑐 1 (𝑑), 𝑐 2 (𝑑) > 0 such that
any 𝑑-regular 𝑘 − 1-edge connected graph 𝐺 with 2𝑛 vertices contains at least 𝑐 1 (𝑑)𝑐 2 (𝑑)𝑛 perfect matchings
and 𝑐 2 (𝑑) → ∞ as 𝑑 → ∞.
   To this date the above conjecture is only proved for 𝑑 = 3 [Esp+11], although the same proof
shows that the conjecture holds for all 𝑑 ≥ 3 as long as 𝑐 2 (𝑑) is allowed to be a ﬁxed constant.
   At a high-level, the study of perfect matchings in general graphs faces the following barriers:
   • Unlike bipartite graphs, the perfect matching polytope of a general graph has exponentially
     many constraints, and it is believed that there does not exist any poly-size convex program
     to test whether a given graph has perfect matchings. This fact signiﬁcantly limits exploiting
     Gurvits’ like techniques [Gur06] in lower-bounding the number of perfect matchings.
   • In a bipartite graph, any odd alternating walk (that starts and ends at un-saturated vertices)
     can be used to extend a near perfect matching to a perfect matching. However, in a general
     graph, an odd alternating walk may contain odd cycles. Therefore, typical augmenting path
     arguments which bound the ratio of near perfect to perfect matchings fail in a non-bipartite
     graph (see e.g., [JV96]).
In this paper we study perfect matchings in regular strong expander graphs: We show that for these
graphs the classical algorithm of [JS89] runs in polynomial time and can generate an approximately
uniform random perfect matching. On the combinatorial side, we prove a signiﬁcantly stronger
version of Conjecture 1.1 for this family of graphs.

EXPONENTIALLY MANY PERFECT MATCHINGS IN CUBIC GRAPHS

                                          LOUIS ESPERET, FRANTIŠEK KARDOŠ, ANDREW D. KING, DANIEL KRÁL’, AND SERGUEI NORINE


                                                 Abstract. We show that every cubic bridgeless graph G has at least 2|V (G)|/3656 perfect matchings.




arXiv:1012.2878v2 [math.CO] 5 Sep 2011
                                                 This confirms an old conjecture of Lovász and Plummer.
                                                    This version of the paper uses a different definition of a burl from the journal version of the
                                                 paper [7], and a different proof of Lemma 18. This simplifies the exposition of our arguments
                                                 throughout the whole paper.




                                                                                       1. Introduction
                                            Given a graph G, let M(G) denote the set of perfect matchings in G. A classical theorem
                                         of Petersen [15] states that every cubic bridgeless graph has at least one perfect matching, i.e.
                                         M(G) 6= ∅. Indeed, it can be proven that any edge in a cubic bridgeless graph is contained in some
                                         perfect matching [14], which implies that |M(G)| ≥ 3.
                                            In the 1970s, Lovász and Plummer conjectured that the number of perfect matchings of a cubic
                                         bridgeless graph G should grow exponentially with its order (see [12, Conjecture 8.1.8]). It is a
                                         simple exercise to prove that G contains at most 2|V (G)| perfect matchings, so we can state the
                                         conjecture as follows:
                                         Lovász-Plummer conjecture. There exists a universal constant ǫ > 0 such that for any cubic
                                         bridgeless graph G,
                                                                      2ǫ|V (G)| ≤ |M(G)| ≤ 2|V (G)| .
                                            The problem of computing |M(G)| is connected to problems in molecular chemistry and statis-
                                         tical physics (see e.g. [12, Section 8.7]). In general graphs, this problem is ♯P -complete [17]. Thus
                                         we are interested in finding good bounds on the number of perfect matchings for various classes of
                                         graphs such as the bounds in the conjecture above.
                                            For bipartite graphs, |M(G)| is precisely the permanent of the graph biadjacency matrix. Voorho-
                                         eve proved the conjecture for cubic bipartite graphs in 1979 [18]; Schrijver later extended this result
                                         to all regular bipartite graphs [16]. We refer the reader to [11] for an exposition of this connection
                                         and of an elegant proof of Gurvits generalizing Schrijver’s result. For fullerene graphs, a class
                                         of planar cubic graphs for which the conjecture relates to molecular stability and aromaticity of
                                         fullerene molecules, the problem was settled by Kardoš, Král’, Miškuf and Sereni [9]. Chudnovsky
                                         and Seymour recently proved the conjecture for all cubic bridgeless planar graphs [1].

                                            The Institute for Theoretical Computer Science is supported by Ministry of Education of Czech Republic as

                                                                                                 1

                   Figure 1. A graph cubic bridgeless graph G with m⋆ (G) = 1.

   The general case has until now remained open. Edmonds, Lovász and Pulleyblank [4] proved
that any cubic bridgeless G contains at least 41 |V (G)| + 2 perfect matchings (see also [13]); this
bound was later improved to 12 |V (G)| [10] and then 43 |V (G)| − 10 [6]. The order of the lower bound
was not improved until Esperet, Kardoš, and Král’ proved a superlinear bound in 2009 [5]. The
first bound, proved in 1982, is a direct consequence of a lower bound on the dimension of the perfect
matching polytope, while the more recent bounds combine polyhedral arguments with analysis of
brick and brace decompositions.
   In this paper we solve the general case. To avoid technical difficulties when contracting sets
of vertices, we henceforth allow graphs to have multiple edges, but not loops. Let m(G) denote
|M(G)|, and let m⋆ (G) denote the minimum, over all edges e ∈ E(G), of the number of perfect
matchings containing e. Our result is the following:
Theorem 1. For every cubic bridgeless graph G we have m(G) ≥ 2|V (G)|/3656 .
    We actually prove that at least one of two sufficient conditions applies:
Theorem 2. For every cubic bridgeless graph G, at least one of the following holds:

                                                                                Fuliang Lu†1 and Fengming Dong‡2

                                                                                              Abstract
                                                         An edge cut C of a graph G is tight if |C ∩ M | = 1 for every perfect matching
                                                     M of G. Barrier-cuts and 2-separation cuts, also referred to as ELP-cuts, are two
                                                     important types of tight cuts in matching covered graphs. Edmonds, Lovász and
                                                     Pulleyblank [Brick decompositions and the matching rank of graphs, Combinatorica
                                                     2(3) (1982) 247-274] proved that if a matching covered graph has a non-trivial tight
                                                     cut, then it also has a non-trivial ELP-cut. In conﬁrmation of a conjecture proposed
                                                     by Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty, Chen et. al. [Laminar tight cuts in matching
                                                     covered graphs, J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B, 150 (2021) 177-194] showed that if C
                                                     is a non-trivial tight cut of a matching covered graph G, then G has at least one
                                                     C-sheltered non-trivial barrier or a 2-separation cut that is laminar with C.
                                                         In this paper, we present a complete characterization of non-trivial tight cuts
                                                     in matching covered graphs, from which the result of Chen et. al. can be derived
                                                     directly. Moreover, we show that the lower bound of the number of C-sheltered
                                                     non-trivial barrier or a 2-separation cut that is laminar with C in the result of Chen
                                                     et. al. is sharp.

                                                   Keywords: matching covered graphs; tight cuts; ELP-cuts.

                                           in X and the other end point in Y . Clearly, ∂(X) := E[X, X] is an edge cut of G for

nonempty subset X of V (G), the subgraph of G induced by X is denoted by G[X]; the
set of all vertices of V (G) \ X that are adjacent to some vertex in X is denoted by NG (X).
Two edge cuts ∂(X) and ∂(Y ) cross if each of X ∩ Y , X ∩ Y , X ∩ Y and X ∩ Y is not

G by contracting X to a singleton x (and removing any resulting loops). The graphs
G/(X → x) and G/(X → x) are ∂(X)-contractions of G.
    A connected non-trivial graph G is matching covered if each edge in G lies in a perfect
matching. An edge cut ∂(X) is tight of G if |∂(X) ∩ M| = 1 for every perfect matching
M of G. A trivial edge cut is obviously a tight cut. A matching covered graph without
non-trivial tight cuts is called a brace if it is bipartite, and is called a brick if it is non-
bipartite. There is a procedure called a tight cut decomposition, due to Lovász [8], which
can be applied to a matching covered graph G to produce a list of unique braces and
bricks. In particular, any two applications of the tight cut decomposition procedure yield
the same number of bricks [8], which is called the brick number of G. Using the tool of
tight cut decomposition, many problems about matching covered graphs can be reduced
to braces and bricks.
    Let G be a matching covered graph. We denote by o(H) the number of odd components
of a graph H. A nonempty vertex set B of G is a barrier if o(G − B) = |B|. An edge
cut C of G is a barrier-cut if there exists a barrier B of G and an odd component Q of
G − B such that C = ∂(V (Q)). A vertex set S of G is a 2-separation if |S| = 2, G − S is
disconnected and each of the components of G − S is even. Let {u, v} be a 2-separation
of G, and let us divide the components of G − {u, v} into two nonempty subgraphs G1
and G2 . The cuts ∂(V (G1 ) + u) and ∂(V (G1 ) + v) are both 2-separation cuts associated
with {u, v} of G. Barrier-cuts and 2-separation cuts, called ELP-cuts, play an important
role in tight cut decomposition (it can be checked that ELP-cuts are tight cuts). The
following theorem, called ELP-Theorem, due to Edmonds, Lovász, and Pulleyblank [5],
is a fundamental result of matching theory.
Theorem 1.1 ([5]). Every matching covered graph that has a non-trivial tight cut has a
non-trivial barrier or a 2-separation.
    The proof of Theorem 1.1 given by Edmonds, Lovász, and Pulleyblank is based on
linear programming techniques [5]. Szigeti [9] provided a purely graph-theoretical proof of
this theorem. Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty [2] gave an alternative proof of ELP-Theorem
by using properties of barriers in graphs that has a perfect matching.

C-sheltered barrier-cut is laminar with C. Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty [2] conjectured
that given any non-trivial tight cut C in a matching covered graph that is not an ELP-cut,
there exists a non-trivial ELP-cut D that is laminar with C, and proved this conjecture
for bicritical graphs and also for matching covered graphs with brick number at most
two. For a matching covered graph G and a non-trivial tight cut C, let ELP G (C) be the
collection of C-sheltered non-trivial barrier-cuts and 2-separation cuts that are laminar
with C. Chen et. al. proved the conjecture of Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty [2], as stated
below.
Theorem 1.2 ([4]). Let C be a non-trivial tight cut of a matching covered graph G. Then
|ELP G (C)| ≥ 1.

contains no 2-separations in F \ {F }.

The famous conjecture of Lovász and Plummer, very recently proven by Esperet et al. (2011), asserts that every cubic
bridgeless graph has exponentially many perfect matchings. In this paper we improve the bound of Esperet et al. for
a specific subclass of cubic bridgeless graphs called the Klee-graphs. We show that every Klee-graph with n ≥ 8
vertices has at least 3 · 2(n+12)/60 perfect matchings.

Keywords: Klee-graphs, perfect matchings, Lovász-Plummer conjecture



1        Introduction
In this paper, we focus on a specific class of planar cubic bridgeless graphs, namely the Klee-graphs,
defined as follows. A graph G is a Klee-graph if G = K4 or there exists a Klee-graph G0 such that G can
be obtained from G0 by replacing a vertex by a triangle (see Figure 1).




                                 Fig. 1: Replacing a vertex by a triangle in a cubic graph.


  For a given undirected graph G, let V (G) be the set of its vertices and let E(G) be the set of its edges.
A matching in a graph G is a set M ⊆ E(G) such that every vertex is an endvertex of at most one edge

in M . A perfect matching is a matching where every vertex is an endvertex of exactly one edge in the
matching.
   Let us now mention a well-known conjecture of Lovász and Plummer [8, Conjecture 8.1.8]
Conjecture 1.1 (Lovász-Plummer) Every bridgeless cubic graph G has exponentially many (as a func-
tion of |V (G)|) perfect matchings.
In 1982, Edmonds et al. [2] proved that every bridgeless cubic graph on n vertices has at least n/4 + 2
perfect matchings. This linear lower bound was improved by Král’ et al. [7] to n/2 and then by Esperet
et al. [5] to 43 n − 10. In 2009 Esperet et al. [4] came up with a deep and complex proof of a first known
superlinear bound.
   Meanwhile, the Lovász-Plummer conjecture has been proven for cubic bipartite graphs by Voorhoeve
[10] and extended to all regular bipartite graphs by Shrijver [9]. Recently Kardoš et al. [6] proved that
fullerene graphs, i.e., planar cubic 3-connected graphs with only pentagonal and hexagonal faces, have a
very large number of perfect matchings — their lower bound is 2(n−380)/61 . A result by Chudnovsky and
Seymour [1] from 2008 shows that the conjecture is true for all planar cubic bridgeless graphs. However,
their exponential bound is very small, namely, they assert that every n-vertex planar cubic graph G has at
least 2n/655978752 perfect matchings.
   The conjecture of Lovász and Plummer was finally proven in 2010 by Esperet et al. [3], who give a
2n/3656 lower bound for the number of perfect matchings in an arbitrary n-vertex cubic bridgeless graph.
   On the other hand, Klee-graphs play important role in the matchings and cubic graphs theory and
therefore obtaining a better bound for the number of perfect matchings in Klee-graphs seems interesting.
Every 3-edge-connected cubic graph that is not a Klee-graph is double-covered (i.e., every edge belongs
to at least two perfect matchings) [5]. Thus, one may expect that Klee-graphs are the 3-edge-connected
cubic graphs with fewest perfect matchings.

3 and finally we do calculations and show that every Klee-graph with n ≥ 8 vertices has at least 3 ·
2(n+12)/60 perfect matchings in Section 4. In Section 5 we provide an upper bound for the number of
perfect matchings in Klee-graphs. More precisely, we show an infinite family of Klee-graphs with at most
c 2n/17.285 perfect matchings, where c is some absolute constant.
